name: Delicata squash
tile_uses: Roasted, pasta, beside salmon, the weekend braise
why_now: September brought the first ones. By October they've cured longer — more orange down in the grooves, sweeter inside — and they cost less. It's the squash in the weekend braise, and the one worth keeping two of on the counter all month.
how_to_choose: Orange in the grooves between the green stripes means longer cured and sweeter
Firm all over, with no soft or wet spots at either end
A dry, intact stem still attached
Small to medium; the large ones get watery
buy_this_much: 3. Two for roasting through the week, one for the pot on the weekend.
price_note: Cheaper than it was in September, and still sold by the piece — the medium ones are the better buy.

flavor_paths.name: Roasted plain
flavor_paths.description: Half-moons, oil, salt, 425°F. Still the version you'll make most.

flavor_paths.name: With pomegranate
flavor_paths.description: Roasted dark, seeds scattered on while it's hot. Sweet against sharp.

flavor_paths.name: Braised
flavor_paths.description: Cut thick and cooked in the pot with chicken and beans. It holds its shape.

weekday_uses: Roasted beside salmon on the same sheet pan
Folded into pasta with butter browned with sage
Cold from the fridge in a rice bowl, with salsa macha
On yogurt with pomegranate and salt
weekend_use: Cut into thick half-moons and braised with bone-in chicken thighs, white beans, poblano, and rosemary — the weekend meal.
storage: On the counter, out of the sun, for a month. It doesn't want the fridge. Once cut, wrap it and use it within four days.
one_thing_to_learn: Delicata holds its shape in a braise where butternut would collapse. The thin skin you don't peel is structure. For the pot, cut it thick — an inch — so it turns tender when the chicken does, not before.
market_question: Which of these has been curing longest?
